analysis.one_liner: Replaces all public and private health insurance with a universal single-payer program.
analysis.headline: The single-payer bill was referred to five House committees and their subcommittees, never got a hearing, markup, or vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would create a government-run health insurance program covering every U.S. citizen and lawful resident, administered by the states under federal standards. It would pay for hospital care, doctor visits, prescription drugs, dental care, mental health care, and long-term care with no premiums, deductibles, or copays and no balance billing. It would end Medicare, Medicaid, the Children's Health Insurance Program, federal employee coverage, TRICARE, and the Affordable Care Act's insurance exchanges, and would ban private insurance that duplicates the program's benefits. It would be financed by a payroll tax on employers, a health care income tax, a surcharge on high-income households, and a tax on securities transactions.
analysis.who_benefits: Every U.S. resident would get comprehensive coverage regardless of job, income, or health status, with no premiums, deductibles, or copays, and no surprise bills from providers. The 51 million uninsured counted in the bill's own findings would gain the most, along with people priced out of dental, mental health, or long-term care. Businesses, especially small ones, would stop paying rising premiums and administering plans — the bill's findings note automakers spend more on health care than on steel.
analysis.who_benefits_short: All U.S. residents and small businesses

how_it_helps.text: Every U.S. citizen, national, and lawful resident alien is entitled to comprehensive health benefits through a state health security program.

Covered services include hospital care, professional services, prescription drugs, dental care, mental health and substance abuse treatment, preventive services, and home and community-based long-term care.
No one may bill a patient for charges beyond what the program pays — eliminating premiums, deductibles, copays, and balance billing for covered services.
Benefits are portable across states, ending the loss of coverage that comes with changing or losing a job.
The bill's findings state that 51 million Americans were uninsured in 2009, the largest single-year increase since 1987, and that rising health bills prevent small businesses from creating jobs.

analysis.who_pays: Employers would pay a new payroll tax and individuals a new health care income tax; households with high incomes would pay a surcharge; and investors would pay a tax on securities transactions. The private health insurance industry would lose its core business, since selling duplicative coverage would be banned. Hospitals would move from billed charges to approved global budgets.

drawbacks.text: The program is financed by a payroll tax on employers, a health care income tax, a surcharge on high-income individuals, and a tax on securities transactions — so some households and businesses could pay more in new taxes than they previously paid in premiums.

The bill ends Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, federal employee coverage, and TRICARE, and repeals the Affordable Care Act's exchanges — a wholesale transition of every American's coverage arrangement at once, with union plans and employer plans limited to supplemental benefits.
States must prohibit the sale of private health insurance that duplicates program benefits, eliminating the option of primary private coverage.

Hospitals would be paid through approved global budgets rather than itemized charges, and utilization review programs would be eliminated — a major change in how health care is priced that providers would have to absorb.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is large and direct: universal coverage with no out-of-pocket costs for covered care, including dental, mental health, and long-term care that most plans limit. The costs are also large and certain: broad new taxes replacing premiums, the elimination of the private primary insurance market, and a one-time conversion of Medicare, Medicaid, employer plans, and the ACA exchanges into a single state-administered program. Honest supporters would concede the transition would be disruptive and that some middle- and high-income households would pay more in taxes than they paid in premiums; honest opponents would concede it insures everyone and removes billing from the doctor-patient relationship. How well the tax burden and provider payment levels were tuned would decide whether it was a good deal for most people.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in five House committees — none ever scheduled it for a hearing or markup — and it died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Rep. Jim McDermott introduced the bill on March 17, 2011, and it was referred to five House committees: Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Oversight and Government Reform, Armed Services, and Education and the Workforce.
Between late March and May 2011 it was further referred to subcommittees on Health, on the Federal Workforce and Labor Policy, on Health Employment Labor and Pensions, and on Military Personnel.
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred before the Congress ended on January 3, 2013.
The only analysis available is the Congressional Research Service summary of the bill as introduced; it never advanced far enough for a cost estimate or a committee-written version.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The existing health care system's main payers and providers came out ahead: private insurers kept their market, pharmaceutical companies kept private-market pricing, and employers kept the current arrangement rather than facing a new payroll tax. The 51 million uninsured named in the bill's findings gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private insurers and the status quo

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 11 cosponsors were Democrats, with no Republican support anywhere in the record, and Republicans held the House majority after the 2010 elections.

industries.note: The bill ends federal employee coverage, repeals the ACA exchanges, and requires states to ban the sale of insurance duplicating program benefits — abolishing insurers' core business and leaving them only supplemental coverage. Insurers profit by standing between patients and care, so eliminating them is the bill's central mechanism for cutting costs.

A single public program would replace fragmented private and public payers with government-set payment for prescription drugs, ending the pricing power that comes from negotiating against many insurers. Drug prices are a leading driver of what patients and taxpayers pay.

Hospitals would be paid through approved global budgets instead of itemized billed charges — likely lower than private-insurer rates, but with guaranteed payment and an end to unpaid bills. Their interest in current private payment rates runs against patients' interest in lower costs.

Businesses would stop buying and administering health plans, though they would pay a new payroll tax; the bill's findings stress that small businesses raising 10–15% a year in health bills cannot reinvest or create jobs.
A tax on securities transactions would help finance the program, directly trimming trading profits. That revenue would fund coverage for everyone.
Practitioners would get guaranteed payment and simplified billing under a prospective fee schedule, but would face mandatory assignment and government-set rates rather than private-market fees.
